notes.text: Learning notes: Daily Trading Challenge

Practise a quick scenario or go deeper with a hypothetical case, labelled visual, 10 linked questions and worked explanations. 50 exercises rotate; new banks are prepared every two months and wait for owner approval. Answers stay on this browser.
Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.
How the daily challenge works

Daily offers a quick hypothetical market scenario alongside a longer ten-question case study. You choose a response, compare the reasoning and trade-offs, then answer a short bonus knowledge question about market basics. Completing the quick reasoning step or all ten case-study questions advances the browser-stored streak at most once per local day. Directional reflections are not forecast scores.

The scenario's prices, news events and dates are exercise inputs, not a report of what happened in today's markets. Choosing long, short or hold records a reflection; it does not place an order. Use the explanation to compare assumptions and uncertainty rather than treating completion as evidence of forecasting skill.
Using a daily habit to support review
Skill in trading comes from repetition and review, and both need frequency.
A small daily task is easier to sustain than a weekly marathon session.
Streaks make the boring parts — journaling, reviewing, sizing — habitual.
After a missed day, resume when your schedule allows; a streak is a participation aid, not a skill grade.
A longer daily practice session

The deeper exercise develops one case across ten linked questions, so the learner can calculate an input, interpret the result and identify a limitation. Topics rotate between portfolio arithmetic, transaction costs and supported orders, price-data freshness, risk and uncertainty, and decision habits. The visuals show selected hypothetical inputs with numeric labels; they are not live market charts. Worked explanations appear after each submitted answer, including when the answer was wrong.

After you finish, the case takeaway provides a review guide for checking the reasoning. Checked answers are saved on this browser. After the first saved answer, the case keeps its own snapshot if a new bank is approved while you are working. Clearing site data removes this local history; an account does not synchronize this case history to another device.

A new 50-exercise bank is prepared every two calendar months in five parts using the configured free-tier Gemini API. Each completed bank remains private and editable in the owner’s admin panel until final review and approval. If generation hits a quota limit, fails validation or awaits review, the approved bank continues rotating. Fifty exercises can therefore repeat before the next bank begins; revisits are review practice rather than a claim of brand-new daily content. The feature does not use a paid provider fallback.
What the challenges cover
A hypothetical market scenario with stated exercise inputs, rather than current market news.
Comparing long, short and hold reasoning without grading one market direction as objectively correct.
A bank of 50 deeper exercises, each with a substantial hypothetical case, a labelled visual and ten linked questions with worked explanations.
The existing short bonus quiz plus a case takeaway with a review guide.
How the streak is counted

A streak advances once per calendar day in your own local time zone, so completing a challenge late one evening and early the next morning still counts as two consecutive days. The counter lives in your browser, which means clearing site data resets it and using a different device starts a separate count even when you have an account; sign-in does not back up local streaks.

There is no penalty for missing a day beyond the counter resetting, and longer streaks unlock browser-local completion badges, not prizes or qualifications. Nothing about the challenge involves money, prizes or entry fees.
If you miss a day

Nothing bad happens beyond the counter going back to one. The purpose of the streak is to make practice frequent, not to punish a missed evening, and restarting after a gap is the normal experience rather than a failure. The counter is not a judgment about you or a measurement of future returns.
If daily practice does not fit your schedule, choose a workable review rhythm. A record of what you learned is more informative than a raw session count.

text: Two unequal positions fall together / brief
content:
Consider $60,000 cash, $30,000 in a stock and $10,000 in a crypto asset. The stock falls 5% while the crypto falls 20%. Treat these as simultaneous hypothetical moves with no trades or fees. Both position losses matter, but averaging the two percentage changes ignores how much money was invested in each.

After the simultaneous declines, consider a follow-up interval: the stock rebounds 5% from its reduced value while crypto rebounds 20% from its reduced value. Cash stays unchanged. Prepare an account-value bridge showing both invested contributions and cash. These selected moves are worksheet inputs, not forecasts. Distinguish each holding’s own return from its contribution to the starting account, and check whether the two rebounds restore the original total.

Your worksheet contains $40,000 in fund A and $60,000 in fund B. Fund A rises 25% while fund B stays flat. Ignore fees and cash flows. You originally assigned fund A a 40% weight. Before deciding whether it is above that target, recalculate both the holding value and the portfolio denominator.

At the new $110,000 portfolio total, examine a separate fee-free rebalance to 40% A and 60% B. Assume value can move between funds at unchanged marks without costs. Determine how much leaves A and enters B. The earlier price gain already belongs to equity; selling some of A does not create that gain again. In execution, an allocation target remains a plan until the appropriate supported orders occur.

text: The planned exit is only a worksheet / brief
content:
A learner holds ten units marked at $50 and writes “exit if the quote reaches $45” in a journal. TradeHQ supports manual market buys and sells, not automatic stop orders. For the arithmetic assume all ten units could be sold at exactly $45 and ignore fees. Then separate that calculation from what the written plan actually executes.

Suppose the learner returns late and the available worksheet quote is $43 rather than the planned $45. Compare both assumed exits, initially excluding fees. Then calculate the fee on a ten-unit sale at $43. The journal condition was never a placed stop order. A calculation about a planned exit cannot guarantee the price available when a manual order is finally submitted.

text: Unsupported does not mean real-time / brief
content:
A hypothetical portfolio holds an asset with a fixed simulator quote of $25. The provider has no usable mapping for that asset. Another holding has a valid provider snapshot. Later that second position rises to $990 while the unsupported mark stays fixed. No trades occur. A classmate claims that a functioning refresh makes both positions live-priced. Check the contribution of each holding and identify what the combined total can and cannot establish.
